readerTitle: FedEx didn't sell shipping. It sold certainty.
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Federal Express, 1970년대 창업기) + 가상 적용 (오피스 상권 식당)
insight: 좋은 가치 제안은 '무엇을 하는가'가 아니라 '고객이 무엇을 잃지 않게 되는가'를 약속하며, 그 약속을 매번 지킬 운영이 뒤따라야 한다.
misconception: 더 싸거나 더 많은 것을 해 주겠다고 하면 고객이 고른다. 약속은 크게 할수록 좋다.

sources.text: FedEx 공식 기업 역사 자료 (1973년 4월 멤피스 허브 운항 개시, 첫날 항공기·도시·화물 수)
Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'FedEx Corporation' 및 'Frederick W. Smith' 항목 (창업, 허브 앤 스포크, 초기 적자)
'When it absolutely, positively has to be there overnight' 광고 캠페인 (Ally & Gargano, 1970년대 후반) 관련 광고사 기록

factChecks.note: 1973년 4월 17일 밤 멤피스 허브에서 운항 개시, 소형 제트기(다쏘 팰컨) 14대, 25개 도시, 첫날 화물 186개는 FedEx 공식 역사 자료 기준입니다. 카드에는 '186 packages'만 'according to company history'로 적었습니다. 게시 전 공식 자료로 다시 확인하세요.
슬로건 문구와 캠페인 시기(1978년경, Ally & Gargano)를 확인하세요. 카드에는 연도 없이 'its ads'로만 적었습니다.
창업 초기 수년간 큰 적자와 자금난을 겪었다는 점은 널리 알려져 있으나 구체 금액은 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다. 라스베이거스 블랙잭 일화, 예일대 학기말 보고서 일화는 과장 가능성이 있어 제외했습니다.
당시 긴급 화물이 주로 여객기 화물칸으로 운송되었고 도착 시점이 불확실했다는 서술은 정성적 묘사입니다. 가까운 두 도시 간 화물도 멤피스를 거쳤다는 점은 허브 앤 스포크 설명에서 흔히 쓰이는 예시이므로 표현을 확인하세요.
팩스와 이메일이 긴급 서류 수요 일부를 대체했다는 내용은 일반적 서술로만 적었습니다. 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: FedEx didn't sell shipping. It sold certainty.
body: In 1973, a small company in Memphis began flying packages across the US overnight. On its first full night, according to company history, it carried just 186 packages.
A few years later, its ads made a promise few shippers dared to make: *when it absolutely, positively has to be there overnight.* That one sentence explains much of what came next.

image.label: A single small cargo jet taking off at night with one glowing parcel
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 밤하늘 아래 작은 화물 제트기 한 대가 이륙하고, 창문 너머로 빛나는 소포 하나가 보임. 실제 FedEx 로고, 보라·주황 도장, 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You're starting an air delivery service.
body: It's the early 1970s. Businesses send urgent items, such as spare parts, contracts and medical supplies, mostly as cargo on passenger flights. Nobody can say for sure when they'll arrive.
What do you build your business around?

options.text: The lowest price for sending things by air
options.feedback: Airlines already fill spare cargo space cheaply. You'd compete where they're strongest, and price shoppers leave the moment someone undercuts you.

options.text: Guaranteed overnight arrival for urgent items, at a premium price
options.feedback: You serve the customers who lose the most when things arrive late. The catch: you must build an operation that keeps the promise every single night.

options.text: Every kind of shipment, big or small, fast or slow
options.feedback: More possible volume, but no clear reason to pick you. A mixed network is also much harder to make reliable.

cards.title: Every package flew to Memphis.
body: Founder Fred Smith chose the urgent customer. Federal Express bought its own small jets and trucks instead of relying on airline schedules.
Each night, planes flew from cities into one central hub in Memphis. Packages were sorted and flown back out before morning. Even a parcel between two nearby cities could go through Memphis.
It looks wasteful. But one hub meant one schedule the company fully controlled, so every city could reach every other city overnight.

image.label: Hub-and-spoke map with every route passing through one central city
image.brief: 단순한 미국 지도 실루엣. 가운데 'Memphis' 허브에서 여러 도시로 선이 뻗어 나감. 가까운 두 도시 사이 소포가 직선이 아니라 허브를 거쳐 가는 경로를 점선으로 강조. 로고 없음.

cards.title: The value proposition
body: A **value proposition** is a clear promise of what a specific customer gets from you, and why it beats their next best option.

FedEx's promise wasn't "we fly packages." It was certainty: your item will be there tomorrow. The slogan named the customer (someone whose shipment *has* to arrive), the benefit (overnight, reliably) and, quietly, the alternative: sending it the usual way and hoping.

cards.title: Why certainty is worth paying for.
body: For the right customer, the shipping price is small next to the cost of being late:
list: A factory line stopped, waiting for one spare part
A signed contract that must arrive before a deadline
A clinic waiting on a supply it needs today
cards.callout: The promise was valued against the cost of failure, not the cost of flying.
cards.softwareNote: Cloud hosting and payment companies make the same kind of promise with uptime commitments. Customers pay for certainty because an outage costs them far more than the monthly bill.

cards.title: A promise is only as good as the system behind it.
body: The slogan worked because the planes, the hub and the trucks were all built to keep it. A bold promise without that system is just a public way to disappoint people.

Keeping it was expensive. Federal Express lost money in its early years and came close to running out of cash. And a promise tied to one job can weaken when that job changes. Fax machines, and later email, took over many urgent documents.

image.label: A bold promise sign held up by a visible scaffold of gears
image.brief: 큰 간판 'Overnight. Guaranteed.'을 뒤에서 톱니바퀴, 트럭, 비행기 모양 비계가 떠받치는 그림. 비계 하나가 빠지면 간판이 기울어질 듯한 긴장감. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Now it's a lunch restaurant.
body: Your restaurant sits among offices. Workers get short lunch breaks, and some go elsewhere because your kitchen is sometimes slow at noon.
A manager suggests a sign: "Lunch in 15 minutes, or it's free." What do you do?

options.text: Put the sign up this week to win customers back
options.feedback: The promise is sharp, but your kitchen can't keep it yet. Every missed lunch costs a free meal and teaches customers not to trust you.

options.text: First build a short lunch menu and prep line that hits 15 minutes almost every day, then make the promise
options.feedback: You give up a few weeks and some menu choice. In return, the promise matches what office workers fear most, and you can keep it.

options.text: Advertise "fast, friendly lunch" without a number
options.feedback: Safe, because you can't break a vague promise. But nearly every restaurant says this, so it gives nobody a reason to switch.

cards.title: Promise what customers can't afford to lose, then build to keep it.
body: FedEx won by naming the customer's fear of being late and building every part of the business to remove it.
**Try it today:** finish this sentence for your business: "When it really has to ___, customers choose us because ___." Then list what in your operations makes that true every time.
